title: Interception overhaul: VPN relay health, TLS handshake failures, HTTP/3 honesty
summary: One design direction built entirely from requestr's existing vocabulary — frosted-glass GlassCards over the iOS-style blurred Interceptr header, uppercase letter-spaced section headers from SettingsScreen, BadgePill/MethodBadge/StatusCodeBadge pills, monospace numerics, and the app's status-color set (green #10B981 healthy/decrypted, amber #F59E0B degraded/pending, red #EF4444 failed/blocked, gray #64748B inactive/unknown). Every screen is drawn at 390x844 with the real Intercept status banner, search bar, method chips, and the tri-state capture FAB, so the build agent can map each block onto an existing composable. All three surfaces are presented in both Obsidian Dark (the app's default themeMode = MONOCHROME_DARK) and Editorial Light, since the app decouples them. Surface 1 puts relay health in the Intercept screen as a collapsed GlassCard (status pill, per-transport flow tiles, relayed-vs-dropped bar, throughput, flow-table line) that expands into a bottom sheet with drop-reason bars, per-address-family IPv4/IPv6 NAT rows, and flow-table pressure; the degraded state names each drop reason so drops are attributable rather than mysterious, and the down state shows honest zeroes plus a route back to capture instead of implying traffic. Surface 2 adds a red FAILED pill with a warning glyph plus a 3px left status rail on TLS rows, so FAILED separates from DECRYPTED (green, lock) and SNI/JA3 ONLY (gray, lock) at a glance even in a dense list; its expanded detail leads with a plain-language headline, then category, which side sent the alert, a three-step handshake-stage rail showing exactly where it died, the raw alert record, and a remedy block whose primary action is the actual fix (Install requestr CA for unknown_ca, Extend cipher set for handshake_failure). Surface 3 gives HTTP/3 three distinct row indicators — green lock-open HTTP/3 (decoded), amber key-off HTTP/3 (observed, no keys), gray QUIC (detected only) — deliberately using amber, never red, so a legitimate no-keys state can never read as a bug; the undecrypted detail states plainly that requestr read every packet and that QUIC payloads are encrypted with handshake-derived keys, shows exactly what was decoded from the Initial packet, and offers the path to decodability. Recommended per section: the dark expanded relay readout, the dark unknown_ca failure detail, and the dark traffic-row indicator set, because those three are the highest-risk judgement calls and dark is the shipped default.
